1.pericope_label: The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John: Who bare record of the word of God, and of the testimony of Jesus Christ, and of all things that he saw. Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand.

schools.summary: Open on the word itself: revelation means an uncovering, the Greek carries no article, so this is a revelation and not the revelation, a title that leaves room for the rest of Scripture; the word is late and rare outside the New Testament, once in Plutarch and current in the vernacular. Settle the genitive against Hort and with Swete, on the ground of the clause that follows, and give three further reasons — that God is said to have given it to him, that it concerns what must shortly come to pass, and that the book in fact discloses events rather than a person. Quote Grotius, that John is the writer but Jesus Christ is the author, and hold that only a living person could be the beginning of creation and its final rest. On shortly, resist the praeterist inference: the words of God are of perpetual fulfilment, having been and being and yet to be fulfilled, so the principles are not spent in the first application; and make the phrase a relative term to be judged by God's clock rather than ours, granting all the same that the early hope did look for a speedy return and that the book must be read by the light of that hope and of the fires of persecution from Rome. Then the beatitude: prefer private reading, since the book was sent abroad to Christians and not only to ministers, and add the honest limit that the promise is not of understanding but of privilege, though no writer could call a man favoured for hearing what meant nothing to him. Or take the reading as public, note that the lector grew into an office, and remark that the reading of Scripture in worship is still often poorly done. Say that the word keep is itself the proof that the fulfilment belongs to no single age, since what is to be kept must be keepable now.

Make the blessing practical before anything else: the book opens by promising blessing to the one who reads and hears and keeps, so that whoever takes pains over the reading may learn from it to do works and keep the precepts. Say that teacher and hearer are blessed together, because a short season of labour is followed by joys that do not end. Give the reason the thing was veiled: he wrapped this revelation in mystical words so that it might not be manifested to all and become lightly esteemed. Explain why it needed revealing at all — the progress by which the Church founded by the apostles was to be extended, and the end in which it was to be perfected, had to be shown in order to strengthen the preachers of the faith against the opposition of the world. Note that John in his own manner refers the glory of the Son to the Father, and testifies that Jesus Christ received this from God; that shortly means what is to happen to the Church in the present time; and that the writer is identified for us as the same man who bore witness to the eternal Word made flesh, saying that we saw his glory. Add that he obtained the sight above all others by the privilege of a peculiar chastity, and that the angel appeared to him in the form of Christ. On the Name, expound the three tenses: he is, because he endures continually; he was, because with the Father he made all things; he is to come, because he will assuredly come to judgment. Find the sevenfold Spirit already in Isaiah, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and piety, and the fear of the Lord; and take the seven churches as written to every church, since seven is the number by which universality is denoted.

Set out the four ways the book has been read and refuse to choose between them: as predicting the fall of Jerusalem and the Roman civil wars; as foretelling persecution under the heathen emperors and peace under the Christian ones; as exposing the Roman pontiffs and the ruin of their system; or as foretelling the destruction of the Reformation, this last invented by way of retaliation, with its boldest advocate naming a year that has since passed while the Protestant churches stand. Canvass the authorship the same way, weighing the apostle, the presbyter and Cerinthus, and dismissing the last on the ground that the Church would never have received a work from a reputed heretic; then decline to add any opinion of your own, refer the reader elsewhere, quote Graserus that the whole book seems so obscure that its explanation can hardly be attempted without danger, and deliver a verdict on the trade itself — that the expositions of this book have done great disservice to religion, since almost every commentator has become a prophet, and disappointment has taught shallow thinkers to despise prophecy altogether. Then set against that the other temper: note that no prophecy in the older Scriptures carries this title, and read the book as a manifesto in which the Heir of all things declares that all power is given him; praise the structure as breathing the art of God, comprising things near and remote, greatest and least, terrible and comfortable, interwoven and opposite, sometimes broken off and suspended and afterwards most seasonably appearing again. Say plainly that some have handled the book so badly that others are afraid to touch it, as if the beatitude ran the other way; and show how much it explains of itself, and how its parts answer to Daniel and Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Zechariah, taking a stock from the old prophets and inserting a new graft.

Ask first whose revelation this is, and answer both ways: either Christ is the author, since it was he who sent and showed it by his angel, and he who took the book and opened its seals; or he is the subject, since it treats so much of his person, offices and grace, and of the state of his church through the ages of time. Take the foreknowledge as a proof of deity, since none but God can foretell things to come or declare the end from the beginning and from ancient times the things that are not yet, which is what is done throughout this book. Then read the beatitude as covering both private and public use — the reading of the book in the closet or the family, carefully and diligently and with a desire to understand it, and the reading of it in the church by one who endeavours to open and explain it to others; and see in the change of number that follows an allusion to the reading of the law and the prophets in the synagogues, which were not barely read but expounded.

Trace the pedigree of the book stage by stage. It is the revelation of Jesus Christ, as the whole Bible is, since all revelation comes through him and centres in him; it is a revelation which God gave to Christ, for though he is himself God, as Mediator he receives his instructions from the Father, and the human nature of Christ, however endowed with judgment and penetration, could not by reason have discovered events that depend wholly on the will of God; Christ sent and signified it by his angel, the angels being God's messengers and Christ's servants; and the angel signified it to John, who was chosen for the service as the last of the apostles and the beloved disciple, so that the last book of divine revelation should be notified to the church by the last of them. Then work the beatitude into steps: that it is a blessed privilege to enjoy the oracles of God at all, one of the chief advantages Israel had over the nations; that those are well employed who search the scriptures; that it is a further privilege not only to read but to hear them read by those qualified to give the sense and lead into an understanding of them; that reading and hearing are not sufficient, since the things written must be kept in memory, in mind, in the affections and in practice, and the blessing lies in the deed; and that the nearer we come to the accomplishment of the scriptures the greater regard we shall give them, so that as we see the day approaching we should be so much the more attentive.

debates.question: Is this a revelation about Christ, or one that Christ gives?

sides.position: One that Christ gives, against those who take the genitive as objective; the next clause requires it
Christ is the author and John only the writer, and only a living person could be the beginning of creation and its final rest
One that Christ gives, on three grounds: God gave it to him, it concerns what must shortly come to pass, and it discloses events rather than a person
Both may be said — he is either the author, since he sent and showed it, or the subject, since it treats so much of his person and offices

debates.question: How is the book to be read?

sides.position: There are four hypotheses and no ground to choose between them; the expositions of this book have done great disservice to religion, since almost every commentator has become a prophet
The words of God are of perpetual fulfilment, so the principles are not exhausted by their first application
The whole structure breathes the art of God, and the book largely explains itself

debates.question: Does the beatitude belong to private or public reading?

sides.position: Private, since the book was sent abroad to Christians and not merely to ministers
Public: the church reader gradually acquired an official position
Both, the closet and the family as well as the church, with an allusion to the reading of the law in the synagogues, which was not barely read but expounded

outliers.note: Alone refuses to interpret at all, setting out four rival hypotheses without choosing, quoting Graserus that the book can scarcely be explained without danger, and then condemning the whole enterprise of commenting on it as a disservice to religion.
Alone reads the beatitude as a working instruction rather than a promise, so that the point of taking pains over the reading is to learn from it to do works.

themes: the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him
blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear

4.pericope_label: John to the seven churches which are in Asia: Grace be unto you, and peace, from him which is, and which was, and which is to come; and from the seven Spirits which are before his throne; And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

schools.summary: Fix the geography first: Asia here is neither the continent nor the peninsula but the Roman province, a strip of seaboard bounded roughly by the Caycus, the Maeander, the Phrygian hills and the sea, of which Ephesus was the chief city; run through the looser senses of the word and set them aside. Note that there were congregations elsewhere in the region — Troas, Colossae, Hierapolis, perhaps Magnesia and Tralles — so the seven were not all there were, but the best points of communication with seven districts, seven being besides a favourite number of completeness in this book. Follow Philo in taking seven as unity developed in diversity, and draw the consequence that the seals, trumpets and vials are not three successive periods but three aspects of one, and that the letters, addressed to real congregations, are the heritage of the Church in every epoch. On the salutation, treat the broken grammar as deliberate rather than illiterate, since the regular construction stands in the very next line: the nominative is left standing on purpose, to call attention to the eternity and unchangeableness of the Name, and there is no will be with an eternal God, so the third term is he that cometh. Set the phrase beside the inscription reported from the temple of Isis at Sais and the oracle in Pausanias, and mark the contrast, since the heathen formula makes God an ever-becoming identified with the universe while this one describes a personal, self-revealing God. Refuse the seven angels: the context admits no meaning but the Spirit, sevenfold in operation, whose gifts are diffused among all the churches. Then read the three titles of Christ as the plan of the book — the Revealing Prophet, the Life-giving High Priest and the real Ruler of mankind — pressing the present tense of the last, since the disposition to dwell on a future reign has obscured a present one. Trace the firstborn to the Messianic psalm, prefer the reading loosed to washed, and mark the change of tense, since he loosed us once but loves us always.

Begin as the Jewish prophets did, noting that they name themselves at the head of the messages they receive, and that this writer does the same. Identify Asia as the Lydian or Proconsular province, name the seven cities, and grant that there were other churches then in Phrygia, Pamphylia, Galatia, Pontus and Cappadocia, so that these seven were simply those nearest and most particularly under his care, though the number seven may also stand for perfection as the Hebrews use their sevens. On the Name, produce the rabbinic parallels — the saying that God told Moses to tell them I Was, I Now Am, and I Will Be in Future, and the reason given for three hours of prayer, that the morning points to him who was before the foundation of the world, the noon to him who is, and the evening to him who is to come — and observe how exactly the threefold form expresses eternity, since we have no idea of time but as past, present and to come. Then divide on the seven spirits. Argue that they are angels, and call it most evident from the place, the number and the tradition, producing Raphael in Tobit as one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints, the Targum where God speaks to the seven angels standing before him, and the rabbinic picture of the throne as the court of an eastern monarch with seven ministers. Or argue the contrary from the book's own usage: that the angels are never termed spirits in it, and that when all the angels stand up and worship, the seven spirits neither stand up nor worship, so that not seven created angels but the Holy Ghost is meant, seven being a sacred number that does not always imply a precise one. On the titles, take the three appellations in their proper order, faithful witness before his death and in it, first fruits of them that slept, and prince — a title he will presently exchange for king — and note that no creature, much less a sinful man, can bear the title of king absolutely before the eyes of God.

Observe the order of naming and give the reason for it: Christ, though the second Person, is mentioned last because many things were to be said of him, and he is described in all his offices at once. On the kingdom and priesthood, gather the readings of the older copies and versions, which give a kingdom, priests, or a kingdom and priests, or a kingdom of priesthood, and refer the whole to the promise that ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, which the Jerusalem Targum renders ye shall be unto me kings and priests, and the other Targum paraphrases as kings crowned with a crown and priests ministering. Add the common saying that all Israelites are the sons of kings, and that the doctors are called kings of the law, and note that the same thing is elsewhere ascribed to the word of the Lord which is here ascribed to Jesus Christ.

Say that there can be no true peace where there is not true grace, and that where grace goes before, peace will follow. Take the blessing as pronounced in the name of the whole Trinity, since it is an act of adoration and God alone is its proper object: the Father named first as the eternal and unchangeable one who is and was and is to come; the Holy Spirit called the seven spirits, the perfect Spirit of God in whom there is a diversity of gifts and operations; and the Lord Jesus Christ, from eternity a witness to all the counsels of God, the first-born from the dead who will by his own power raise up his people, and the Prince of the kings of the earth, by whom their counsels are overruled and to whom they are accountable. Then press the doctrine of the blood: sin leaves a stain of guilt and pollution on the soul, and nothing can fetch out that stain but the blood of Christ, who shed his own to satisfy divine justice and purchase pardon and purity for his people. Say what the kingship and priesthood amount to in practice — that as kings believers overcome the world, mortify sin, govern their own spirits, resist Satan and prevail with God in prayer, and that as priests they have access to God and offer spiritual and acceptable sacrifices — and conclude that for such favours they are bound to ascribe dominion and glory to him for ever.

Raise the thought higher than those who confess one God and stop there. They admit by their doctrines that God is one, whatever their idolatries have often denied, but they do not admit that he is also the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; and in this they are of a contrary mind to their own prophets, who affirm in the Divine Scriptures that the Lord said, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. Say that they rage and gather themselves together against the Lord and against his Anointed to this day, supposing it possible to be made friends of the Father apart from devotion towards the Son, and being ignorant that no man comes to the Father but by the Son, who says, I am the Door, and I am the Way. Ask how one who refuses the Way that leads to the Father, and denies the Door, shall be deemed worthy of entrance to God. Then bring the psalm against them, where the son says, He shall call me, Thou art my Father, my God, and the helper of my salvation, and where the promise follows that God will make him his firstborn.

debates.question: What are the seven Spirits before the throne?

sides.position: Seven angels — most evident from the place, the number and the tradition, with Raphael in Tobit and the Targum on the seven who stand before God
The Holy Spirit, since angels are nowhere called the Spirits of God and such language could not be proper of a creature
The Holy Spirit, sevenfold in operation; the angel reading is plainly untenable whatever names support it
The Holy Ghost, since angels are never termed spirits in this book, and when all the angels stand up and worship the seven spirits neither stand nor worship
The perfect Spirit of God, in whom there is a diversity of gifts and operations

debates.question: Is the broken grammar of the divine Name a blunder?

sides.position: No: the regular construction stands in the very next line, so the nominative is deliberate, to mark eternity and unchangeableness
No: it is the deliberate putting in emphatic form of the Name of Names, and should be preserved in English
It is a wonderful rendering of the great name, purely Jewish in phraseology

debates.question: Does the salutation echo the inscription of Isis at Sais?

sides.position: The parallels are worth citing — the Sais inscription, Orpheus, the oracle in Pausanias
The parallel is real but the point is the contrast: the heathen inscription makes God an ever-becoming identified with the universe, this one a personal self-revealing God

outliers.note: Alone holds out for seven angels against the rest, and is named by Barnes among the advocates of that view before being answered.
Alone draws a structural conclusion from the number seven, arguing from Philo that the seals, trumpets and vials are not three successive periods but three aspects of one.

themes: him which is, and which was, and which is to come
the seven Spirits which are before his throne
hath made us kings and priests unto God

7.pericope_label: Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him, and they also which pierced him: and all kindreds of the earth shall wail because of him. Even so, Amen. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty.

schools.summary: Hear the coming as a reminiscence of Daniel and treat it as a common eschatological refrain, comparing the manifestation of God in the clouds at Sinai, in the cloudy pillar and at the transfiguration; note that cloud is a fit emblem of majesty even among the heathen, who clothed their gods the same way, and that the whole design of the picture is to impress the rank and glory of the one from whom these disclosures come. Keep the piercing wide enough to cover any looking upon the pierced one, whether at the cross, or afterwards by faith, or by the sinner who reflects that his crimes caused that death. Then handle the text closely: the verb for pierced occurs only here and in the Fourth Gospel, in both places out of the same prophet but in neither from the Greek version, which is evidence that the writer used the Hebrew or one of the later translators; and the verb for mourning means to cut oneself, as mourners did. Take the tribes not of Israel only but of the spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles, and add that no nation had then accepted Christ as Lord, nor has any since. Draw out the difference from the prophet, who described the mourning of grief over one dead, whereas here the mourning is directed towards one who was dead and is alive, so that those who wail are turning to him the sorrow they owed him at the tomb. On the last verse, give the rabbinic background that from aleph to tav meant a thing entire, so that Adam transgressed the law and Abraham kept it from aleph to tav; judge the clause about the beginning and the ending to be no part of the text but an importation from the book's closing chapter; grant that the language could belong to none but the true God and that the natural reference is to Jesus, yet decline to use the verse as a proof of his divinity, since the manuscripts now preferred read God where the received text reads Lord. Or resolve it the other way, noting that the speaker changes without announcement and that only here and in one later place is God himself brought in speaking, his eternity standing as the guarantee of the prophecy just made.

Refer the coming to judgment on the enemies of the religion, and probably to the destruction of Jerusalem, since he was to be manifested particularly to them that pierced him, which must mean the incredulous and rebellious Jews. Read all the kindreds of the earth as all the tribes of the land, take the whole verse as predicting the destruction of the Jews, and treat it as presumptive proof that the book was written before the final overthrow of the Jewish state. Or take the coming otherwise, as always in this book meaning the glorious coming, whose preparation began at the destruction of Jerusalem and goes on without interruption until the event is accomplished, which is why it is never said that he will come, nor that he cometh again, but always that he cometh — for when he came before it was in the form of a servant, and only his appearing in glory is properly his coming. Make it a rule that the word tribes in this book always means the Israelites, while granting that where another word such as nations or peoples is joined with it, as here, the rest of mankind is included. Then on the title, borrow from the Jews, who expressed the whole compass of a matter by their first and last letters, and accommodate it to the Greek alphabet, citing the sayings that Adam transgressed the law from aleph to tav and Abraham observed it from aleph to tav. Report that the clause about the beginning and the ending is wanting in almost every manuscript and version of importance, appears to have been added as an explanatory note and crept into the text, and has been struck out by Griesbach. Observe finally that the two Hebrew letters joined make a word the rabbins interpret of the first matter of all things, while the two Greek letters joined make the verb to breathe, which is apt in a symbolic book for him in whom we live and move and have our being.

Rule out the readings that make this coming anything but personal. It cannot be his coming to take vengeance on the Jews at the destruction of Jerusalem, though that event is sometimes described in such language, because if the revelation was made in the latter end of Domitian's reign, as the ancients commonly report and the chronologers generally place it, it must fall upwards of twenty years after that destruction. Nor can it be a coming in a spiritual sense to convert the Jews in the latter day, for this coming is personal, and with clouds, and he will be seen by every eye; besides which, all the kindreds of the earth would not lament on such an occasion, since the wicked would take little notice of it, the tribes of the Jews would rejoice at it, and so would all the converted Gentiles. On the title that follows, take the words as Christ's own, spoken to confirm what has just been said of his person, offices and future coming: the first letter and the last of the alphabet, signifying that he is the first and the last, a character often given to the divine Being in the prophetic writings, and no small proof of the proper deity of Christ; and note that the first letter is used by the Jews for the chief of persons or of things.

debates.question: Is the coming with clouds the fall of Jerusalem or the last advent?

sides.position: Jerusalem: all the tribes of the land means the Jewish people, and this is presumptive proof the book predates the overthrow of the Jewish state
Not Jerusalem: on the received dating the vision falls more than twenty years after it, and a conversion would not set all the kindreds of the earth lamenting
Neither exclusively: the preparation began at the fall of Jerusalem and goes on uninterrupted, which is why the book never says he will come but always that he cometh

debates.question: Who are the tribes that wail?

sides.position: The Israelites, as always in this book, though a word for nations joined with it takes in the rest of mankind
Not the Jewish tribes but the spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles

debates.question: Does the title Alpha and Omega prove the divinity of Christ?

sides.position: It is no small proof of the proper deity of Christ
The words are a strong declaration of his divinity

The language could belong to none but the true God, and the natural reference is to Jesus, but the verse cannot be adduced as a proof-text, since the preferred manuscripts read God where the received text reads Lord
Only here and in one later place is God himself brought in speaking, the change of speaker being unannounced

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse against the present, adding that no nation had then accepted Christ as Lord and Saviour, nor has any yet done so.
Alone declines to use the Alpha and Omega as a proof-text for the divinity of Christ, on textual grounds, while agreeing the language could belong to none but the true God.

9.pericope_label: I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ. I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and heard behind me a great voice, as of a trumpet, Saying, I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last: and, What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia.

schools.summary: Notice what the writer does not call himself: the absence of the title apostle is not evidence against his being one but self-effacement and oneness with his readers, as in the Fourth Gospel, and in apocalyptic writing the personality of the writer is always prominent to guarantee the visions. Observe that a single article binds tribulation, kingdom and patience into one picture, all three being present realities and ideas that run through the whole book, and that the patience is neither for Christ nor of Christ but draws its life and energy of endurance from him. Describe Patmos soberly — a rocky, sparsely settled island some ten miles long and half as wide, one of the Sporades, south of Miletus — and remark how little of its scenery colours the book, so that at the farthest one thinks only of the blue water flushing and flashing in the light. Take his position there as that of an exile free to move within the island, with no chains or guard such as Paul had, and give the cause of the exile in his own words, the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. Then define the state he was in: he came to be in the Spirit, that is, into an ecstatic condition and not the normal spiritual state — or, against the others, deny the prophetic ecstasy altogether, on the ground that the command to make a record came only afterwards, and hold that this was rather a high state of religious enjoyment such as any Christian may experience. Rule out the futurist reading of the day, which would make it the day of judgment, since the phrase is quite different; note that the adjective was applied first to the Lord's Supper and passed from the supper to the day, that the Levant calls it so still, and that the papyri show the same word meaning imperial, the first of each month being Emperor's Day when payments fell due, so that Christians took over a term already in use. On the command, mark that it covers the whole series of visions, and that the order of the seven runs north from Ephesus and then east and south, though the whole book was to be read, and probably copied, at each.

Describe the island at length, since its name is all most readers know of it: one of the Sporades in the Aegean between Icaria and the promontory of Miletus, now called Patino or Palmosa, with a convent on a well fortified hill dedicated to the apostle, about three hundred men and some twenty women to every man, very barren and producing little grain but abounding in partridges, quails, turtles, pigeons and rabbits, with many good harbours and much infested by pirates, and about thirty miles in circumference. Leave the emperor undecided, weighing Domitian, Claudius and Nero, and incline to the last; or name Domitian and Nerva instead, and make the place itself the point, since he had Asia and the seven churches over against him at a small distance, Jerusalem and Canaan beyond, Rome and Europe to the west, Alexandria and the Nile and all Africa to the south, so that the three known parts of the world lay before his eyes as a theatre for the scenes to pass over, the island serving as an observatory. Say that the book peculiarly belongs to those under the cross, since it was given to a banished man and men in affliction understand and relish it most, and trace its fortunes accordingly, little esteemed by the Asiatic church after Constantine but highly valued by the African churches and by the persecuted since. Take the being in the Spirit as a trance, so overwhelmed with the power and filled with the light of the Spirit as to be insensible of outward things, and insist that what follows is one single connected vision seen in one day, whose parts depend exactly on each other, so that the reader should carry his thought straight through without interruption. Have him facing east, towards Asia and the churches he must write to, and the trumpet peculiarly proper to proclaim the coming of a great king; and note that though every book of the New Testament was written by the will of God, none other was so expressly commanded to be written.

Mark where the narrative proper begins, the preceding verses being a general preface and these the introduction to the first vision. Take the self-description as deliberate: he names himself, being well known to the seven churches and giving them no reason to doubt his fidelity, and he calls himself their brother not in a natural but in a spiritual sense, so that though an elder, an evangelist, yea an apostle by office, he puts himself on a level with the several members of these churches as a believer in Christ. Then argue the day. It is not the Jewish sabbath, which was now abolished and was never called the Lord's day, and had that been meant he would have said the sabbath day; nor is it the passover; it is the first day of the week, as one version renders it outright, called the Lord's day just as the supper is called the Lord's supper, because on it he rose from the dead and on it he appeared to his disciples, and because the primitive churches set it apart for his worship and met on it to hear the word. Cite Justin Martyr, who lived within about fifty years, for the practice: on the day the Greeks call Sunday the Christians met together in one place, read the Scriptures, prayed together and administered the supper. On the disputed title in the last verse, grant that it is left out by the Alexandrian copy, the Complutensian edition and the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic versions, but keep it as very fitly retained, to point out the person who speaks, to express his dignity, deity and eternity, and to give weight to what he says.

Take the account of the man before the account of the vision. He describes himself by his present state, as brother and companion of these churches in tribulation and in the kingdom and patience of Christ: a persecuted man, banished and perhaps imprisoned for his adherence to Christ; their brother, though an apostle, seeming to value himself on his relation to the church rather than his authority in it, since Judas Iscariot may be an apostle but not a brother in the family of God; their companion, because the children of God should choose communion and society with each other; their companion in tribulation, since the persecuted servants of God do not suffer alone and the same trials are accomplished in others; and their companion in patience, a sharer not only in suffering circumstances but in suffering graces, so that if we have the patience of the saints we should not grudge to meet with their trials. Observe that by this account of his own condition he acknowledges his engagement to sympathise with them and to give them counsel and comfort, and bespeaks their more careful attention to what he has to say from their common Lord. Then note the place, the isle of Patmos, and note also what he leaves out: he does not say who banished him thither, since it becomes Christians to speak sparingly and modestly of those who wrong them.

debates.question: What state was the seer in?

sides.position: An ecstatic condition, not the normal spiritual state
A trance, so overwhelmed as to be insensible of outward things
The Spirit of prophecy, under whose influence the first vision was exhibited
Not the prophetic ecstasy at all, since the command to write came afterwards, but a high state of religious enjoyment such as any Christian may experience
Domitian, Claudius or Nero — most probably the last
Domitian and Nerva
The writer does not say, and it becomes Christians to speak sparingly of such things

debates.question: Should the disputed title in the last verse be kept?

sides.position: No: the whole clause is wanting in the chief manuscripts and versions, and Griesbach has left it out
No: the previous words are not found in the best manuscripts, nor the words which are in Asia
Yes: though left out by several copies and versions, it is very fitly retained, to point out the person who speaks and to give weight to what he says

outliers.note: Alone denies that the seer was in prophetic ecstasy, arguing from the fact that the command to write came only afterwards, and reduces the state to a high degree of ordinary religious enjoyment.

Alone makes the island itself an observatory, placing Asia, Jerusalem, Rome, Alexandria and the northern straits at the four quarters of the seer's view, as though Patmos had been made for the purpose.

themes: your brother and companion in tribulation
I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day
what thou seest, write in a book

12.pericope_label: And I turned to see the voice that spake with me. And being turned, I saw seven golden candlesticks; And in the midst of the seven candlesticks one like unto the Son of man, clothed with a garment down to the foot, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle. His head and his hairs were white like wool, as white as snow; and his eyes were as a flame of fire; And his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters. And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength.

schools.summary: Settle first how many lampstands stood there. Deny that the scene reproduces the prophet's vision of one stand with seven branches, since here the bearers are seven, standing apart and far enough from each other that the figure could stand among them, and nothing in the arrangement suggests the temple. Or reconcile the two: what was seen was very likely the old familiar branched candlestick, the one made known to everyone by the Arch of Titus, but with the seven churches fresh in the mind the eye fell on the seven limbs and lights rather than on the stand — especially if the figure standing there concealed part of the main stem — so that the separate individuality of the churches and their real union in the one Light are shown together. On the figure, insist that the phrase is like a son of man and not like the Son of man, since the Greek has no article and the received rendering would make the writer say that Christ was like himself: he is like a son of man, but is not a man. Read the long robe and the high girdle as priestly, naming him the King-Priest and the Melchisedec of the epistle, and note from Josephus that girding high was itself a mark of dignity in the high priest, the girdle sitting not at the loins as if ready for toil but at the breast, in the repose of sovereignty. On the white head, refuse the reading that makes the whiteness mere radiance, since wool and snow are poor images for brightness and the description follows the Ancient of Days; and answer the objection that age implies decay by pointing to the wigs of monarchs and judges, since the white head is never in public sentiment other than the venerable sign of ripe knowledge and mature judgment. Then the metal: a word found nowhere else, perhaps a white brass, perhaps the old electrum, perhaps a hybrid of Greek and Hebrew meaning brass whitened in the furnace and current in the trade vocabulary of a city of metalworkers — or, more honestly, an unknown metal. Take the sword for the word of God, the only weapon needed, so that whoever takes another to advance the kingdom will perish by the one he chose.

Correct the translation before anything else, since it is absurd to speak of a golden candlestick when lamps are meant, and these seven lamps represent the seven churches, in which the light of God was continually shining and the love of God continually burning, and are called golden to show how precious they were in the sight of God. Refer them to the temple at Jerusalem, where there was a chandelier of seven branches, three springing out on either side and one in the centre, and take the reference as intimating that the temple was a type of the whole Christian Church. Read the vision as coming gradually — first the voice, then the candlesticks set in a circle, then in the midst of them one in human form, then the robe and the golden girdle, both of them marks of royal as well as priestly dignity, girding at the breast being the emblem of solemn rest, since it is the man on a journey who girds his loins. Say that the apostle then looked up to behold the face and was beaten back by the flaming eyes, so that he observed the feet instead, and only afterwards, receiving strength, saw the stars and the sword, and at last the brightness of the countenance, and fell as dead. Take the white head for antiquity, wool being commonly supposed an emblem of eternity and snow betokening spotless purity, but explain the whiteness itself as the rays of glory encircling the head, the splendour the Romans called a nimbus and painters have set about the heads of gods and saints in almost every nation. Identify the metal with the famous aurichalcum, called by one authority a kind of amber more precious than gold, the Corinthian brass that ran together, so the story goes, when Mummius burnt the city and the statues of three metals melted into one; or take it more plainly for copper fused with calamine, and say that you have often stood over those underground furnaces and seen the flame burst up through the earth, which always brought this description back to mind.

Guard the person first. He who stood among the candlesticks was not an angel, for he speaks of himself as the first and the last, phrases not applicable to any created being, and of having been dead and living again and having power over death and the grave, which no creature has. Nor was it the human nature that was in the midst of the churches, but the Son of God appearing in a form like that individual human nature which was at his Father's right hand, as before his incarnation he was said to be like unto the son of man in the older vision to which this refers. Take the white head for his antiquity, since he is the everlasting Father whose goings forth were of old, and for his gravity and prudence, since with the Ancient is wisdom, and for his glory, being the brightness of his Father's glory, and for his proper deity, this description being the same as that of the Ancient of days; and note the Jewish usage by which white wool means the wool of a lamb just born, about which a cloth is bound that it may not be defiled. Read the burning feet of the power by which he bears up and defends his people, or of his providential dealings with them, which are holy and just and will be manifest, or of his wrath in treading down his enemies. Then give the reasons ministers are compared to stars: for their efficient cause, God, who made them and fixed them in their place; for their matter, being of the same nature with the heavens as ministers are with the churches; for their form, receiving their light from the sun as preachers receive theirs from Christ; for their multitude and variety; and chiefly for their usefulness, to give light and point out the way of salvation. Add the Targum's saying that the seven lamps in the candlestick answer to the seven stars to which the righteous are likened.

Say what the candlesticks are for: the churches receive their light from Christ and the gospel and hold it forth to others, and being golden they should be precious and pure, ministers and members alike, their light so shining before men as to engage others to give glory to God. Then read the figure feature by feature as a description of the Mediator. He appeared in the midst of the golden candlesticks, being with his churches always to the end of the world, filling them with light and life and love. The robe down to the feet may represent his righteousness and priesthood; the golden girdle may denote how precious are his love and affection for his people; the head and hairs white like wool and as snow may signify his majesty, purity and eternity; the eyes as a flame of fire may represent his knowledge of the secrets of all hearts and of the most distant events; the feet like fine brass burning in a furnace may denote the firmness of his appointments and the excellence of his proceedings; the voice as the sound of many waters may represent the power of his word, to remove or to destroy. Take the seven stars as emblems of the ministers of the seven churches, whom Christ upheld and directed, and the sword as his justice and his word, piercing to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit.

debates.question: Was there one lampstand or seven?

sides.position: Seven, standing apart, so that the figure could stand among them; the scene is not the temple
A reference to the seven-branched stand at Jerusalem, intimating that the temple was a type of the whole Christian Church
Probably the old branched candlestick, seen limb by limb because the seven churches were fresh in mind and the figure hid part of the stem
Here the lampstands are separate

debates.question: Is the whiteness of the head age or radiance?

sides.position: Radiance: the rays of glory encircling the head, the splendour the Romans called a nimbus
Age: wool and snow are poor images for brightness, and majesty is best signified by one venerable in years
Age, and the objection that it implies decay is answered by the wigs of monarchs and judges
Antiquity, wool being an emblem of eternity and snow of spotless purity

debates.question: What is the metal of the feet?

sides.position: A white brass; the Vulgate's aurichalcum, or the old electrum of four parts gold to one of silver
The Corinthian brass that ran together when Mummius burnt the city, or simply copper fused with calamine
A hybrid of Greek and Hebrew meaning brass whitened in the furnace, a trade word current in a city of metalworkers
In reality an unknown metal

outliers.note: Alone attempts to reconcile the one lampstand with the seven, suggesting that the figure standing in the midst concealed part of the main stem.
Alone reports having watched the furnaces himself, saying that the flame bursting up through the earth from copper fused with calamine always brought this verse back to him.

his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength

17.pericope_label: And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me, saying unto me, Fear not; I am the first and the last: I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death. Write the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter; The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.

schools.summary: Explain the collapse before explaining the comfort. The effect is the one that regularly attends a vision of God, as with Daniel, who was in a deep sleep on his face toward the ground until he was touched and set upright; and doubt whether the apostle recognised the Saviour at once, since some sixty years had passed and the subsequent questions rather imply that he did not. Or read the fall as the felt consciousness of unworthiness, distinguishing it from the pity that made Dante fall as a dead body falls, setting beside it the pagan tale of Semele consumed in the brightness she asked to see, and then turning the fear into evidence, since the man who said he was not worthy that Christ should come under his roof was told that such faith had not been found in Israel. Note that the epithets which follow, the first and the last and the Living One, are used in the older Scriptures of God and are here applied purposely to Jesus. Correct the order of the two nouns at the end, since death comes first and then the unseen realm into which death ushers men, both of them now under his power; insist that the second death is not in view; and picture that realm as a walled city or prison house whose keys are the emblem of authority, as we honour a man by giving him the keys of a city. Find two wonders standing together, that the living One became dead and the dead One is alive for evermore. Then take the threefold commission as the plan of the book, allowing the middle term the wider sense of the eternal principles underlying human history as well as the present state of the churches, and warning that nothing can be argued from the phrase about how long the future runs, though it seems to stretch far. On the angels, canvass the readings — guardian angels, hard to reconcile with words of warning and reproof; the ideal embodiment of the congregation; the chief pastor, which the star imagery favours and which is generally adopted; and the plain sense of messenger — noting that the title was applied to the president of the synagogue. Reject the prelatical reading point by point, and close by quoting a defender of prelacy conceding that the angel may stand for the order of presbyters.

Match the collapse to the prophets, since the appearance of the glory of the Lord had the same effect on Ezekiel and the appearance of Gabriel on Daniel, and the terrible splendour of such majesty was more than the apostle could bear. Then make the contrast personal: before the passion he was intimate enough to lean on that breast and lie in that bosom, yet now, near seventy years after, the aged apostle is struck to the ground by one glance — from which draw the rule that a great sinking of nature usually precedes a large communication of heavenly things, and the exhortation that sinners be afraid and cleanse their hands while saints be humble and rejoice with reverence. Observe that the hand laid on him was the same that held the seven stars, that he is not called by name as the angels called Zechariah but addressed as by a well known master, and that his look terrifies while his speech strengthens; observe too that in the state of humiliation he spoke of his glory in the third person, but now speaks of it without any veil. Take the key for power and authority, and produce the rabbinic parallels: the Jerusalem Targum's four keys in the hand of God which he never trusts to angel or seraph, of the rain, of provision, of the grave and of the barren womb, and the three keys another tract says are not given into the hand of the apostle, of life, of rain and of the resurrection of the dead. Conclude from these that the second word here means merely the grave, and neither hell nor the place of separate spirits — or divide it instead, the body abiding in death and the soul in the unseen, both at his disposal — and then press the consequence: Peter was given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, but not the keys of death or of the unseen; how then does his supposed successor at Rome come by the keys of purgatory? Map the threefold commission onto the chapters exactly, and note that in each church there was one pastor or ruling minister to whom the rest were subordinate, who must answer for those souls.

Take the fall first as a matter of position, since the glorious person described was just behind him and he had now a full view of him. Then hold the titles that follow to their strictest sense. He that liveth is the eternal God, who has life in himself originally, essentially and inderivatively, and who is the fountain and author of life to others; he ever lived as Mediator and Redeemer, and still does, and ever will, and did so even when he was dead as man. On the command, note the reading of some copies that gives write therefore, and confine the first clause to what he had now seen — the vision of one like to the son of man amidst the golden candlesticks, with seven stars in his right hand — rather than to anything he had seen of Christ in the days of his flesh. Then read the last verse as an instruction about writing rather than about stars, since what he is bidden to write is the mystery of them, that is, their mystical sense.

sides.position: Probably not: sixty years had passed, and the later revelations imply he did not
He is addressed not by name, as the angels addressed Zechariah, but as by a well known master
The question is rather what the sight cost him: was this he in whose bosom he had lain at the Last Supper?

debates.question: How far do the keys reach?

sides.position: To the grave only, and neither to hell nor to the place of separate spirits; the rabbinic keys are of rain, provision, the grave and the barren womb
To death and then to the unseen realm death ushers men into; not to the second death
To the body abiding in death and the soul in the unseen — and Peter was given the keys of the kingdom, not these
To a realm conceived as a walled city, the keys being the symbol of authority

debates.question: What are the angels of the seven churches?

sides.position: Not guardian angels, which will not square with words of reproof; most probably the chief pastor, as the star imagery favours
Simplest is the plain sense of messenger, whether sent from the churches or to them
Not prelatical bishops: no such groupings existed, each city has a church in the singular, and on that reading seven bishops replaced one at a stroke
One pastor or ruling minister in each church, to whom the rest were subordinate

outliers.note: Alone turns the keys into a polemic, observing that Peter was given the keys of the kingdom and not these, and asking how his supposed successor at Rome comes by the keys of purgatory.
Alone argues the ecclesiastical question at length, dismantling the prelatical reading of the angels point by point and closing with a concession quoted from a defender of prelacy.
